resources.string: How Steady Health works
The whole app in four short paragraphs.

Four abilities, three things a day. The app keeps track of four things your body does: getting up, going, carrying, and staying steady. Those sit at the top of every day. Under them are the three small things: weigh in whenever it suits you. Say how the day went, in a sentence. Move for two minutes, or longer if you want. When a thing is done it turns green and stays done. The empty days are just days.

Your weight is one of the levers, not the point. It gets smoothed, so one heavy morning doesn't move it. It matters because eighteen fewer pounds is eighteen fewer pounds to lift, every time you get yourself up, and the app says it that way.

Your sessions get longer on your terms. After two that felt easy, the next one is offered. You can say not yet as often as you like. If you're sore the next day, the app suggests something shorter. That's how bodies build.

Everything stays on your phone. There is no account, no server, and no copy anywhere else. If you turn on the optional reader, it runs on your phone too, and it only ever sorts your words and writes your Sunday note. It never sees your weight and never gives advice.

Once a month there's a short check. Ten minutes, with whatever is already in the room. It tells you what you can do now and what it was before. Staying the same counts.
this app\'s own rules, which are open source.
Why the scale jumps overnight
Four pounds overnight is water, not fat.

A salty dinner holds water. A big meal is still on its way through. A hard walk leaves your muscles holding extra fluid while they repair. Where you are in a cycle changes water too. Any of these can move the scale two, three, four pounds by morning.

Fat is different. Gaining or losing a pound of fat takes days of eating more or less than your body uses. It cannot happen overnight. So a jump in the morning number is almost never what it looks like.

That's why Steady shows the smoothed number first. It takes every morning into account and moves slowly, so the water swings mostly cancel out and what's left is the real direction.
normal day-to-day body weight variation is around one to two kilograms; see the Hacker\'s Diet by John Walker for the smoothing method.
Why weight goes flat
A flat stretch around month six is normal and expected.

Most people's weight comes down fastest in the first few months, then slows, then goes flat for a while, often around six months in. This is not a sign that something stopped working. As weight comes down, the body uses a little less energy at rest, appetite tends to come up, and daily movement can quietly drop. The line levels out.

Changing diets does not change this. A 2024 study switched people between diets at the plateau and the flat stretch stayed flat.

What does keep moving is what you can do. Walks get longer, standing up gets quicker. Steady shows those beside the weight line for exactly this reason.
Stanford crossover trial, Scientific Reports, 2024; real-world data from 667 programme users showing decrease, plateau, and partial regain as the most common pattern.
Does two minutes really count?
Short bouts add up, and people keep doing them.

Yes. A 2025 review of eleven trials found that bouts of five minutes or less, done a couple of times a day, improved fitness in adults who had been inactive. Total time was often under half an hour a week. And 83 percent of people stuck with it, which is rare for any exercise study.

A separate study of 25,000 people who did no formal exercise found that about four minutes a day of brisk everyday movement, like climbing stairs quickly or walking fast to the bus, was linked to a noticeably lower chance of dying over the study period.

The barrier was never the minutes. It was believing they had to be more.
Rodriguez et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2025; Stamatakis et al., Nature Medicine, 2022.
How intermittent fasting works
An eating window, not a magic hour.

Intermittent fasting means eating only during certain hours, often eight hours a day, or eating very little on some days. Studies that compare it with simply eating less across the whole day find about the same weight change. Most of its effect comes from eating less overall, not from the timing. What matters most is whether you can keep it up.

It is not for everyone. Skip it if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, if you take insulin or certain diabetes tablets, if you have ever had an eating disorder, or if you are under eighteen. If you take any regular medication, ask whoever prescribes it before changing when you eat.

Steady Health does not track eating windows and will not suggest one.
reviews comparing time-restricted eating with continuous calorie reduction; see the 2022 New England Journal of Medicine trial by Liu et al.
Muscle and weight-loss medications
When weight comes off fast, some of it is muscle. Two things protect it.

On medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide, a meaningful share of the weight lost can be muscle rather than fat. In one large trial it was close to half; in another about a quarter. Losing muscle makes it harder to stand up, carry things, and keep weight off later.

Two habits protect most of it. Something with protein at most meals, and some strength work, like standing up from a chair or wall push-ups, a couple of times a week. That's the whole reason the strength sets in this app exist.

Steady Health never tracks the medication itself. Your doctor's tools do that better.
Neeland et al., Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, 2024, reporting lean mass changes in the STEP-1 and SURMOUNT-1 trials.
Why the app shows a smoothed number
So one heavy morning doesn\'t feel like a verdict.

Smoothing takes every morning's weight into account and gives the newest one only a small say. The result moves slowly and follows the real direction. Day-to-day water swings mostly cancel out.

Research on people who weigh themselves daily finds it helps, but only when the daily swings don't discourage them. The smoothed number is what makes daily weighing bearable.

If you would rather see no numbers at all, there is a switch in settings. The app then uses words like "a little lower" instead.
exponentially weighted moving average as described in the Hacker\'s Diet; self-weighing evidence from a 10,000-user cohort in JMIR, 2021.
Why there are no calories here
Counting works for some people and hurts others. Steady leaves it out.

Calorie apps turn every meal into a number to beat, and a study of nearly 60,000 posts about the biggest ones found the same feelings over and over: shame, blame, and giving up. Among people with eating disorders, most said the most popular calorie app made things worse.

Steady Health tracks what your body can do, your walks, your weight, and how your days go. That's enough to see what's changing. If a food pattern matters, it shows up in your own words, in the Sunday note, without a number attached.

If food is a struggle right now, the resources page in settings has a helpline. No questions asked.
Bondaronek et al., British Journal of Health Psychology, 2025; Levinson et al., Eating Behaviors, 2017.
How a good pace feels
If you can talk but not sing, you\'re at a good pace.

After a walk, Steady asks whether you could have held a conversation. That\'s a real measure, not a guess. If you could talk easily, the pace was gentle. If you could talk but had to catch your breath, it was moderate, which is where most of the benefit is. If you couldn\'t talk, it was hard.\n\nFor most people, most of the time, the moderate pace is plenty. The app uses your answers to decide when to offer a longer walk, and it never pushes past \"just about.\"
the conversation measure as a marker of the first ventilatory threshold, validated in work supported by the American Council on Exercise.
Why walks get longer slowly
Big jumps cause injuries. Small steps don\'t.

The old advice was to add ten percent a week. A study of over five thousand runners found that what actually predicts injury is a single session that's much longer than anything you've done in the last month. A big jump, not a steady climb.

So the app never offers a walk more than about ten percent longer than your longest one in the past thirty days, and only after two walks that felt easy. Repeating a walk is progress. Saying not yet is fine.

If you're sore the next day, the app suggests a shorter one. Bodies build in the rest between, not during.
Frandsen et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2025.
What to do after a break
Ease back in. Nothing is lost.

A week off changes nothing; often it helps. After two or three weeks, breathing fitness has slipped a little but strength is mostly still there. After a month or more, both have slipped, and the tendons and joints take longer to catch back up than the muscles do, which is why the first couple of weeks back are when people get hurt.\n\nSo after a break, the app suggests a slightly shorter walk than where you left off, for a couple of weeks, then opens up again. Your weight line and your history are exactly where you left them.
detraining reviews on aerobic and strength loss over one week to several months.
Why staying the same counts
Holding a number for a year is not nothing.

Most apps only celebrate going up. But muscle strength drops by somewhere between one and a half and five percent a year from midlife onward if nothing is done about it. So a chair-stand count that is the same in December as it was in March is not a flat line. It is a year of that drop not happening.\n\nThat is why this app reports Same the same way it reports Better. If you are holding a number, you are doing the work.
reviews of age-related muscle and strength loss from midlife.
Why the app asks what you want to be able to do
Because a number only means something next to a life.

Physical therapists use a simple tool: the person names three to five things they are struggling with, and rates each out of ten. It is one of the better ways to measure whether treatment worked, because the person picks what counts.\n\nThis app does the same. You said what you wanted; the app tracks those things and asks again once a month. Seven seconds off a chair-stand time is abstract. Getting off the floor without your hands is not.
the Patient-Specific Functional Scale, used widely in physical therapy.
Why strength comes before cardio after fifty
Walking keeps your heart in shape. It does not keep your legs.

Walking is good for your heart, your head and your sleep, and this app asks for plenty of it. What it does not do much of is keep muscle. Muscle needs something heavier than your own easy pace, which is what a chair stand or a push against a wall is.

From around fifty onward, adults lose roughly one percent of muscle a year if nothing pushes back, and strength goes faster than size does. Resistance work reverses a good part of that at any age. A meta-analysis of nearly two thousand adults over fifty found real gains in strength from two or three short sessions a week, in people who had never trained before.

That is the reason the sessions in this app are mostly not walking, and the reason two minutes of standing up from a chair earns its place next to a twenty minute walk.
Peterson et al., Ageing Research Reviews, 2010, a meta-analysis of resistance training in adults over fifty.
Balance is a skill, not a gift
It is trained the way a language is, and it is specific.

People talk about balance as something you have or you do not. It is closer to a skill: it improves with practice, it fades without it, and it is oddly specific. Standing on one leg gets better at standing on one leg. Turning your head while you walk gets better at turning your head while you walk. Practising one does surprisingly little for the other.

That is why the balance work here changes shape as it goes: feet together, then one foot in front of the other, then one leg, then one leg while looking around. Each is a slightly different skill, and the last of them is the one that matters on a real pavement.

A Cochrane review of 108 trials found that the exercise that helps most is the kind that challenges balance directly, done for at least three hours a week in total. Not a lot of hours. Just the right hours.
Sherrington et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2019.
What usually happens after an operation
The first weeks feel worse than the trajectory is.

After a joint replacement or an abdominal operation, most people lose a noticeable amount of strength in the first week or two, more than the operation itself accounts for. Bed rest does most of it. Then it comes back, usually faster than it went, and usually not in a straight line.

Moving early is now the standard almost everywhere. Enhanced recovery programmes get people sitting up and walking within a day or so of many operations, because lying still costs more than the movement does.

What this app can do is keep a record of what you actually managed, day by day, so that at your next appointment you have something better than a memory. What it cannot do is tell you what is safe for your operation. That is a question for whoever did it, and they will have a clear answer.
Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Society guidelines, and studies of muscle loss during short periods of bed rest.
What a physiotherapist actually does
Working out what is limiting you, then giving you something to do about it.

A physiotherapist watches you move, works out which part of it is the limit, and gives you a small number of things to practise. Most of the value is in the programme they leave you with rather than in the appointment itself. Occupational therapists do something related, aimed at the tasks of a day: getting in and out of a bath, dressing, cooking.

How you get one varies. In many countries you can go straight to one privately without being sent. Through a public health service you usually need a referral from a doctor, and there is often a wait. Some workplaces and insurers cover a course of it. It is worth asking rather than assuming.

If you already have a programme from one, this app can hold it. Photograph it, or say it, or type it, and it becomes your session, exactly as they set it.
scope of practice as described by the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy and the American Physical Therapy Association.
How to raise mobility with a doctor
Three sentences, prepared, beat ten minutes of hedging.

Mobility is easy to leave out of an appointment, because it comes on slowly and there is no single moment to describe. Doctors are also more likely to act on something concrete than on the word slowing.

What tends to work is three sentences. What changed. When it started. What it stops you doing. "I could get off the floor in March and now I cannot. It came on over the summer. I have stopped gardening because of it." That is a different appointment from "I have been feeling a bit stiff."

If you have been using this app for a while, the monthly check gives you the first two sentences with numbers attached, and the page you can make for a therapist gives you all three on paper.
the shape of a useful history as clinicians are taught to take one: what changed, when, and what it prevents.
Shoes and staying steady
Indoors is where most people are least well shod.

The shoe research is more consistent than most: a low heel, a thin firm sole you can feel the floor through, a back that holds your heel, and a fastening. Thick soft soles feel comfortable and make it harder to tell where the ground is. Backless slippers come off at the worst moment.

Indoors is the gap. Plenty of people wear sensible shoes to go out and walk around the house in socks or loose slippers, which is where a lot of the time is spent. A pair of indoor shoes that fasten is one of the cheaper changes anybody makes.

This app does not sell anything and has no opinion about brands.
Menz and colleagues, research on footwear characteristics, gait and balance in older adults.
Protein and muscle, plainly
Older bodies need a bit more of it, spread through the day.

Muscle is built and broken down continuously. Protein at a meal tips it briefly toward building. Two things change with age: the tipping takes a larger amount of protein than it used to, and many people eat almost all of theirs at one evening meal.

An expert group looking at this recommended around one to one and a quarter grams per kilogram of body weight a day for healthy adults over sixty five, which is more than the old general figure, and suggested spreading it across meals rather than loading the evening. Roughly, that means something with protein at breakfast and lunch too, not just dinner.

This app does not count anything you eat and will not start. It is mentioned here only because strength work without enough protein is half the job.
Bauer et al., the PROT-AGE Study Group, Journal of the American Medical Directors Association, 2013.
What morning stiffness usually is
How long it lasts matters more than how bad it feels.

Stiffness on getting out of bed is very common and mostly ordinary. Joints hold a little more fluid overnight and the tissues around them are less pliable until they have been moved. It usually eases within ten or fifteen minutes of moving about, and moving is what eases it.

The length is the thing worth noticing. Stiffness that lasts well over an hour most mornings is a different pattern, and it is one of the things clinicians have long asked about specifically, because it points somewhere else. So does stiffness that is much worse on one side, or that comes with a swollen warm joint.

None of that is something an app can sort out, and this one will not try. It is worth a sentence at your next appointment if it fits you.
the 1987 American College of Rheumatology criteria, which used an hour of morning stiffness as one marker, which is why the duration is the part worth noting.
Getting up off the floor, in stages
A sequence worth knowing before you need it. Almost nobody is taught it.

Most people have never been shown how to get up from the floor, and work it out under pressure. It is a sequence, and it is easier once you know the order.

One. Stay where you are for a moment and take a few breaths. Nothing is improved by rushing this part.

Two. Roll onto your side, then push up onto your forearm and then your hand, so you end up sitting on one hip with your hand on the floor.

Three. Get onto all fours, hands and knees, and look around for something solid. A sturdy chair, the bottom stair, a bed frame. Something that will not slide.

Four. Crawl to it. Put both hands on it, bring your stronger leg forward so you are kneeling on one knee with the other foot flat, like a proposal.

Five. Push through that front foot and your hands together, and stand up. Then sit down on the thing you just used, and stay there for a minute.

Practising it is the point, and practise it with a chair, on a rug or a mat, with somebody nearby the first time or two, and going down slowly rather than getting down any way you can. The half kneel to stand and floor to stand movements in the library are this sequence broken into parts you can build up.
the sequence taught by physiotherapists and occupational therapists: side lying, side sitting, four point kneeling, half kneeling, stand.
Why the app measures grip
It is the easiest honest window onto strength everywhere else.

Grip is measured so often in research for a dull reason: it is quick, it needs one cheap instrument, and it tracks strength in the rest of the body reasonably well. Somebody with a strong grip usually has strong legs, not because the hand does the work, but because whatever built one tended to build the other.

It is also one of the first things people notice going. Jars, bags, the handrail on a bus. Those are real losses, and they are trainable: squeezing something, carrying something, holding a band.

This app has no instrument, so it uses what it can watch instead: how long you can carry something, and how many band pulls you can do. Those move for the same reasons.
Leong et al., The Lancet, 2015, the PURE study of grip strength across seventeen countries.
Sore the day after, and what it means
Stiff and aching is ordinary. Sharp, one sided, or swollen is not.

Muscle soreness a day or two after doing something new is ordinary and settles in a few days. It is more about novelty than damage: the same session that leaves you sore in January leaves you fine in March. It is dullest at rest, spread across a whole muscle, and eases as you move.

What is not that: pain that is sharp, that arrived during the movement rather than the next morning, that sits in one joint rather than across a muscle, that is much worse on one side, or that comes with swelling or heat. That is worth stopping for and worth mentioning.

In this app, pressing Something hurts and naming where takes everything that asks a lot of that area out of your sessions for a week, without asking you to explain yourself. Nothing about it is held against you afterwards.
delayed onset muscle soreness as described in exercise physiology; the distinguishing features are duration, location and whether it began during or after.
Sleep, energy, and why the app asks
One question a day, and it only ever speaks if there is a pattern.

Short sleep changes how hard the same effort feels. In laboratory work, people who slept badly rated identical exercise as harder and gave up sooner, without their bodies performing much differently. The effort was the same. The feeling was not.

That is worth knowing on a day when a session that was fine last week feels heavy. It is often the night before rather than the body.

The app asks one optional question a day, two taps, and does nothing with it unless a pattern is real. If one is, it turns up in what the app noticed as a plain observation and nothing more. There is no sleep number here and there never will be.
studies of sleep restriction and perceived exertion, in which performance changes little and how hard it feels changes a lot.
